blocks.html: Most people feel a little shy before they talk to someone new: at a party, on the first day of a club, or while waiting for practice to start. Here is a secret: the other person is often just as nervous, and they will be glad you went first. Starting a conversation is a small kindness you can learn.
Open with a greeting and a simple question or comment about something you share right now: the class, the game, the food, the place. “Hi, I’m Ruby. Have you been to this pool before?”

Manners are kindness made into habits. A friendly opener puts the other person at ease: it shows you are interested in them, and a question about the moment you share is easy for anyone to answer. Nobody has to think hard about “What did you think of the movie?” right after the movie.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.prompt: Sam doesn’t know anyone at his cousin’s party except his cousin. Hana is standing by the snack table. What could Sam say?

choices.text: “Hi, I’m Sam. These pretzels are great. How do you know Ruby?”
say: I’m Hana! We’re on the swim team together.
choices.outcome: A greeting, a comment about the snacks they are both eating, and an easy question. Hana has something to answer.

choices.text: Nothing. He waits for Hana to talk first.
choices.outcome: They both wait, and nobody talks. Someone has to go first; it may as well be Sam.

choices.text: “I got a new bike and it has twenty-one gears.”
choices.outcome: A fact about yourself is hard to answer. Hana can only say “Oh.” A question about something you share works better.

blocks.cap: Try each choice to see how Hana reacts.

blocks.title: At a new club
blocks.q: Leo arrives at the first meeting of the chess club. A girl is setting up a board by herself. What can Leo say?
steps: Start with a greeting and your name: “Hi, I’m Leo.”
Add a question about the thing you share, the club: “Is this your first meeting too?”
If she answers, you have a conversation. If she is quiet, ask one more easy question: “Do you want to play a game?”
blocks.a: “Hi, I’m Leo. Is this your first meeting too?”

blocks.title: A grown-up at a family party
blocks.q: Omar is next to his aunt’s neighbor, Mr. Diaz, at a cookout. What is a good opener?
steps: Greet him with his title: “Hi, Mr. Diaz.”
Comment on or ask about the cookout you are both at: “Did you try the corn? It’s really good.”
Grown-ups enjoy being asked about things, too: “How do you know my aunt?”
blocks.a: “Hi, Mr. Diaz. Did you try the corn?”

blocks.html: Waiting for the other person to start, or opening with a fact about yourself (“I have a new phone”). Waiting leaves you both stuck, and a fact gives them nothing to answer. Check your opener: does it end with a question they can answer easily?
Good openers to keep ready: “How do you know (the host)?” “Have you been here before?” “What did you think of the game?” “Is this seat taken?”

blocks.html: Once you have started a conversation, the next question decides whether it keeps going. Some questions open a door. Others close it.

Open questions begin with words like what, how, why and tell me about, and they invite a real answer: “What was the best part of your trip?” Yes-or-no questions (“Was your trip fun?”) often get one word and a silence.

A good question tells the other person, “I’m interested in you.” An open question gives them room to share a story, and their story gives you the next question. A string of yes-or-no questions starts to feel like a quiz.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: What do you like to do after school?
Do you like school?
cards.why: It can be answered with “Yes” or “No.”

cards.text: How did you get into skateboarding?
Was the movie good?
cards.why: Try “What was your favorite part of the movie?”

cards.text: Tell me about your new puppy!
Is that your dog?
cards.why: A fine start, but follow it with an open question.

blocks.cap: Sort the questions, then Check.

blocks.title: Turning a closed question into an open one
blocks.q: Mia wants to ask Grandpa Walt about his old job. She was going to ask, “Did you like being a mail carrier?” How could she ask it so he has more to say?
steps: “Did you like…” can be answered with one word.
Start with “what” or “tell me” instead.
“What was the funniest thing that happened on your route?” invites a story.
blocks.a: “What was the funniest thing that happened on your mail route?”

blocks.title: Follow the answer
blocks.q: Sam asks Hana, “What did you do this weekend?” Hana says, “We went to the lake.” What is a good next question?
steps: Use what she just said. The lake is the new topic.
Ask an open question about it: “What did you do at the lake?”
Avoid jumping to a new topic of your own; that tells her you were not listening.
blocks.a: “What did you do at the lake?”

blocks.html: Asking a string of yes-or-no questions (“Do you have a dog? Do you like soccer? Is your teacher nice?”) and then running out of things to say. Check: could the answer be one word? Then turn it into a what, how or why question.
Asking questions that pry. Good questions are about interests, plans and opinions, not about money, weight or private family matters. More on that in Topics to Skip.

blocks.html: After you ask a good question, the most important part comes next: listening to the answer. Listening well is a skill, and people can tell right away whether you have it.
Good listeners look at the speaker, let them finish, and ask a follow-up question about what they just said. “You went camping? What did you cook over the fire?”

When someone feels heard, they feel respected. A follow-up question is proof that you listened, because you can only ask it if you were paying attention. It also keeps the conversation going without you having to think up a new topic.

blocks.name: et-scene

say: My grandma taught me to make dumplings this weekend!

choices.text: “That sounds fun! Were they hard to fold?”
say: So hard! Mine looked like little rocks.
choices.outcome: Omar asked about what Ruby just said. Now she has a story to tell.

choices.text: “I went to a basketball game this weekend.”
choices.outcome: Omar jumped to his own story. Ruby can tell he was waiting for his turn, not listening.

choices.text: He nods and looks at his phone.
choices.outcome: Looking away tells Ruby that the phone matters more than she does.

blocks.cap: Choose what Omar says, and watch Ruby’s face.

blocks.title: A follow-up question
blocks.q: Leo tells Sam, “I’m learning to play the drums.” Write a follow-up question for Sam.
steps: Find the new information: Leo is learning the drums.
Ask about it with an open question.
“How long have you been playing?” or “What song are you learning?”
blocks.a: “What song are you learning first?”

blocks.title: When someone is sad
blocks.q: Hana says, “My cat is sick, and we have to take her to the vet.” What does a good listener do?
steps: Look at Hana and let her finish.
Show you heard the feeling: “Oh no, I’m sorry.”
Ask gently, if she seems to want to talk: “What’s her name?” Don’t change the subject to your own pet story.
blocks.a: “Oh no, I’m sorry. What’s her name?”

blocks.html: Spending the other person’s turn planning your own story, then saying “That reminds me…” and talking about yourself. A quick check: before you share your story, have you asked at least one question about theirs?

Customs differ. In the U.S., looking at the speaker’s face shows you are listening. In some families and cultures, looking down a little is the respectful way to listen to an older person. Both are ways of showing respect; more in Eye Contact.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: You know how to listen well. Now put talking and listening together. A good conversation is a game of catch: you catch the ball, hold it for a moment, and toss it back.
Say a little, then toss it back with a question. Keep your turns about as long as the other person’s, and bring quiet people in: “Omar, you play the trumpet, right?”

A conversation belongs to everyone in it. When one person does all the talking, the others feel like an audience instead of friends. Sharing the talk makes each person feel that their ideas matter too.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Answering a question, then asking “What about you?”
Telling a ten-minute story while friends wait to talk.
cards.why: Tell the short version and let others ask for more.

cards.text: Asking the quiet new kid what they think.
Turning every topic back to your own team.
cards.why: Let the topic stay on your friend for a while.

cards.text: Saying “Sorry, go ahead” when you both start at once.
Talking over someone to finish your point.
cards.why: Wait for a pause. Your point will keep.

blocks.cap: Sort each habit, then Check.

blocks.title: Toss it back
blocks.q: Ms. Park asks Ruby, “How was your summer?” Ruby went to camp. How can she answer and share the talk?
steps: Answer with a short version and a detail: “Great! I went to a camp by a lake and learned to canoe.”
Toss it back: “How was yours?”
If Ms. Park wants to hear more, she will ask.
blocks.a: “Great! I learned to canoe at camp. How was your summer?”

blocks.title: Bringing someone in
blocks.q: Leo, Mia and Sam are talking about a video game. Sam has not said anything. What can Mia do?
steps: Notice who has been quiet.
Ask a question that is easy for Sam to answer, about something he knows: “Sam, you like building games, right? What are you playing now?”
Then listen to his answer, just as you would anyone else’s.
blocks.a: “Sam, what are you playing these days?”

blocks.html: Answering one question with a long story and never asking one back, or steering every topic to yourself. A quick check: count your questions. If you have asked none in a few minutes, toss the ball back.

blocks.html: When you share a conversation, some topics bring people together and some make them want to leave. A remark can be true, and even meant kindly, and still make someone uncomfortable.

Leave out remarks about someone’s body or weight, money (how much things cost, how much people earn, how big their house is) and private family matters. Talk about interests, plans, books, games, animals, food and what you are doing together.

People can’t easily change their body, their money or their family’s troubles, and a remark about them puts the person on the spot in front of others. Good manners mean thinking about how a remark will feel to the person who hears it, not only whether it is true.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: What book are you reading?
“You got so tall! You’re huge now.”
cards.why: Even meant kindly, it makes someone think about their body.

cards.text: How much did your sneakers cost?
cards.why: Money questions put people on the spot.

cards.text: What are you doing this summer?
“Why are your parents getting divorced?”
cards.why: A private family matter. Let your friend bring it up if they want to.

cards.text: Which team do you think will win?

blocks.cap: Sort the topics, then Check.

blocks.title: A remark that is true
blocks.q: At a family dinner, Leo notices his cousin has a cast on her arm. Is it fine to ask about it?
steps: A cast is something she will expect questions about, and a kind question shows care.
Keep it gentle and let her decide how much to say: “Oh no, what happened? Does it hurt?”
Skip jokes about it, and don’t ask more if she changes the subject.
blocks.a: Yes, gently: “Oh no, what happened?” Then let her lead.

blocks.title: Steering away
blocks.q: Ruby’s friend says, “Your house is so small!” What could Ruby say, and what is the lesson for the friend?
steps: Ruby can answer calmly and change the topic: “It’s cozy. Want to see my room?”
The friend’s remark was about money and size: it can make a family feel judged.
Better: say something kind and true, like “I love your room!”
blocks.a: Ruby: “It’s cozy. Want to see my room?” The friend: skip remarks about the size of someone’s home.

blocks.html: Thinking a remark is fine because it is true or meant kindly, like “You got so tall!” or “You’ve gained weight.” If it is about someone’s body or money, skip it. A good test: would you want this said about you in front of everyone?

Customs differ. Families differ about what is private. Some talk openly about money at home, and that is their choice. With friends, neighbors and guests, the polite custom in the U.S. is to leave those topics out unless the other person brings them up.

blocks.html: Every conversation ends. When you have shared the talk for a while and need to go, ending well is part of being polite. Many people stay stuck because leaving feels rude. It isn’t, if you do it kindly.
Wait for a pause, then give a kind closing line with a reason if you have one, and say goodbye: “It was good to talk with you. I need to find my mom. See you Monday!”

A friendly closing line tells the other person you enjoyed talking and that you are leaving because you have to, not because of them. It lets you both move on without hurt feelings, and it makes the next conversation easier to start.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: Ending a conversation
items: Wait for a pause in the talk.
Say something kind about the conversation: “It was fun to hear about your trip.”
Give a reason if you have one: “I need to help set up.”
Say goodbye with their name: “See you later, Sam!”
Smile or wave as you go.

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order, then Check.

blocks.title: Leaving a group
blocks.q: Omar is talking with friends after a game and sees his dad waving from the car. What can he say?
steps: He doesn’t need to wait long; a parent waiting is a good reason.
Closing line with the reason: “My dad’s here. Great game, everybody!”
Goodbye: “See you at practice!”
blocks.a: “My dad’s here. Great game, everybody! See you at practice!”

blocks.title: A grown-up who keeps talking
blocks.q: Mr. Diaz, a neighbor, has been telling Hana about his garden for a long time, and Hana promised to help Grandma June in the kitchen. What can Hana do?
steps: Wait for a pause instead of breaking in mid-sentence.
Say something kind: “Your tomatoes sound amazing, Mr. Diaz.”
Give the reason and leave warmly: “I promised to help Grandma in the kitchen. It was nice talking with you!”
blocks.a: “Your tomatoes sound amazing. I promised to help Grandma, so I’d better go. It was nice talking with you!”

blocks.html: Walking away in the middle of someone’s sentence, or staying stuck because leaving feels rude. Wait for a pause, then use a closing line. Check: did you say something kind and say goodbye?

blocks.html: Sooner or later you will meet someone and nobody will be there to introduce you: a new neighbor, a teammate’s parent, a substitute teacher. That is your chance to introduce yourself, and it takes about five seconds.
Stand, smile, look at the person, say your name clearly (“Hi, I’m Leo”), and add one detail that gives them something to talk about: “I’m Sam’s cousin” or “I just joined the team.”

A clear name is a gift: the other person doesn’t have to guess or ask again. The detail tells them how you fit in, and it hands them an easy way to keep talking. Standing and looking at them shows that you think meeting them matters.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: Introducing yourself
items: Stand up if you are sitting.
Smile and look at the person.
Say hello and your name clearly: “Hi, I’m Ruby.”
Add a detail: “I live next door.”
Listen for their name and say, “Nice to meet you.”

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order, then Check.

blocks.title: Meeting a new coach
blocks.q: Hana arrives at her first swim practice. The coach, Mr. Diaz, doesn’t know her yet. What can she say?
steps: Walk up, smile and look at him.
Say her full name, because a coach needs it for the team list: “Hi, Mr. Diaz. I’m Hana Kim.”
Add a detail: “I’m new this season.”
blocks.a: “Hi, Mr. Diaz. I’m Hana Kim. I’m new this season.”

blocks.title: At a friend’s house
blocks.q: Omar goes to Leo’s house for the first time, and Leo’s grandmother opens the door. Leo is upstairs. What should Omar say?
steps: Greet her and say who he is: “Hello, I’m Omar.”
Add the detail that explains why he is there: “I’m Leo’s friend from school.”
If she says her name, use it: “Nice to meet you, Mrs. Hale.”
blocks.a: “Hello, I’m Omar, Leo’s friend from school.”

blocks.html: Mumbling your name while looking down, so it has to be asked again. Say it clearly, at a normal pace, while you look at the person. A quick check: could someone across a table hear and spell your name?
With grown-ups, giving your full name (“I’m Sam Rivera”) is helpful. With kids your age, a first name is fine.

blocks.html: When you introduce yourself or listen to someone, your eyes say a lot. In the U.S., looking at a person’s face tells them, “I’m interested, and I’m paying attention.”

Look at the person’s face while you greet them and while you listen. Glance away now and then, the way people naturally do. Don’t stare without blinking, and don’t keep your eyes on the floor the whole time.

People feel respected when they can see that your attention is on them. Eye contact is one of the clearest signals of attention, so in American custom it goes with greeting, thanking and listening. A soft, friendly look puts people at ease; a hard stare does the opposite.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Looking at Grandma’s face while she tells a story.
Staring without blinking for the whole conversation.
cards.why: A stare feels like a contest. Glance away now and then.

cards.text: Looking up and smiling when you say thank you.
Watching your phone while the coach talks to you.
cards.why: Your eyes show where your attention is.

cards.text: Glancing away for a moment while you think.
Looking at the floor during the whole introduction.
cards.why: Try looking up for your name and the person’s.

blocks.cap: Sort each habit, then Check.

blocks.title: Saying thank you
blocks.q: Mr. Diaz hands Sam a trophy at the team party. How can Sam use eye contact?
steps: Look up at Mr. Diaz’s face as he takes the trophy.
Smile and say, “Thank you, Coach.”
Then he can look at the trophy; nobody expects a long stare.
blocks.a: Look at Mr. Diaz, smile and say thank you.

blocks.title: When it feels hard
blocks.q: Ruby feels nervous looking right into people’s eyes. What can she do?
steps: She can look at the person’s face, near the eyes or at the nose; it looks the same from the other side.
Looking up for the greeting and the goodbye covers the most important moments.
Practice with family first, where it feels easy.
blocks.a: Look at the face, near the eyes, especially for hello, thank you and goodbye.

blocks.html: Staring without blinking, or never looking up at all. Both make the other person uncomfortable. Aim for a friendly look at the face, with natural glances away.

Customs differ. In some cultures and families, looking an older person straight in the eye can seem bold, and looking down a little is the respectful way. If a friend or a grown-up looks away while you talk, they may be showing respect in their own way. Neither way is wrong; each is a way to honor the other person.

blocks.html: A handshake often goes with introducing yourself. Grown-ups may offer you a hand when you meet them, at a game, a job fair, a ceremony, or when your parent introduces you. A good handshake takes a little practice and lasts about two seconds.
Stand, reach out your right hand, meet the other hand palm to palm, grip firmly but not hard, shake two or three times, and let go. Look at the person and smile while you do it.

A handshake is a small, friendly promise: “I’m glad to meet you, and I mean it.” A firm grip shows you are paying attention; a crushing one feels like a contest and a limp one feels like you would rather not. Standing shows the moment matters.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: A good handshake
items: Stand up and face the person.
Smile and look at them.
Reach out your right hand, thumb up.
Meet palm to palm, so the skin between your thumb and finger touches theirs.
Grip firmly and shake two or three times.
Let go and say, “Nice to meet you.”

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order, then Check.

blocks.title: Meeting a friend’s dad
blocks.q: Leo’s friend Omar says, “Dad, this is Leo.” Omar’s dad reaches out his hand. What should Leo do?
steps: Stand if he is sitting.
Take the hand palm to palm with a firm grip and shake two or three times.
Look at him, smile and say, “Nice to meet you, Mr. Haddad.”
blocks.a: Stand, shake firmly two or three times, and say, “Nice to meet you, Mr. Haddad.”

blocks.title: After a game
blocks.q: Mia’s team lost. The teams line up to shake hands. What does a good handshake look like here?
steps: Walk the line and offer each player a quick handshake, or the low five the league uses.
Say “Good game” to each person.
Keep it friendly and short, win or lose. More in Sportsmanship.
blocks.a: A quick shake or low five and “Good game,” to every player.

blocks.html: A limp “fingertip” shake, a bone-crushing squeeze, or staying seated. Check: did your palms meet? Was it firm, like holding a full glass, and not tight like squeezing a lemon?

Customs differ. Not everyone shakes hands. Some people prefer not to for reasons of culture, religion or health, and many cultures greet with a bow, a nod, a hand on the heart or a kiss on the cheek. If someone does not offer a hand, smile and say hello instead. Nobody has to touch anyone to be polite.

blocks.html: When you introduce yourself, the other person tells you their name. A few seconds later, many people have already forgotten it. Here is how to keep it.
Repeat the name right away (“Nice to meet you, Grace”), use it once more before you say goodbye, and if you missed it, ask again soon: “I’m sorry, could you tell me your name again?”

A person’s name matters to them. Using it tells them you cared enough to remember. Saying it out loud also helps your memory hold on to it. And asking again right away is easy and polite; waiting weeks makes it much more awkward.

blocks.name: et-scene

say: Hi, I’m Ruby Walsh. I’m in your third-period art class.
Nice to meet you, Ruby. I’m Ms. Park.
Nice to meet you, Ms. Park.
frames.narr: Ruby repeats the name right away. Saying it out loud helps her remember it.

say: Thanks for showing me the room, Ms. Park. See you Monday!
frames.narr: She uses the name once more as she leaves.

blocks.cap: Use Next to watch Ruby learn and use her new teacher’s name.

blocks.title: Repeat it right away
blocks.q: At a family picnic, Sam meets his uncle’s friend. She says, “Hi, I’m Priya.” What should Sam say?
steps: Use the name in your answer: “Nice to meet you, Priya.”
If grown-ups usually go by a title in your family, ask: “Should I call you Ms. Shah?”
Use it once more when you leave: “Bye, Ms. Shah!”
blocks.a: “Nice to meet you, Priya.” (or “Ms. Shah,” if that is what she prefers)

blocks.title: When you forgot
blocks.q: Ten minutes after meeting a new teammate, Hana realizes she has forgotten his name. What should she do?
steps: Ask now; it only gets harder later.
Say it kindly and take the blame: “I’m sorry, I missed your name. Can you tell me again?”
Repeat it right away when he answers: “Omar. Got it. Thanks, Omar.”
blocks.a: “I’m sorry, I missed your name. Can you tell me again?”

blocks.html: Being too embarrassed to ask for a name again, so you avoid using it for weeks. Everyone forgets names. Asking right away is easy and polite; the awkward part is waiting.

Memory tricks: link the name to a picture (“Grace with the green scarf”), or to someone you know with the same name. And if someone seems to have forgotten yours, help them out: “Hi, I’m Leo. We met at the game.”

blocks.html: Once you know how to remember and use names, you can do something kind for two people who haven’t met: introduce them. There is a simple order that etiquette writers have used for more than a century.

Say the name of the older or honored person first, then present the other person to them. Then introduce the honored person back, and give each one a detail to talk about: “Grandma, this is my friend Omar. Omar, this is my grandmother, Mrs. Hale. Omar plays chess too.”

Saying someone’s name first is a small way to honor them: it shows respect to an older person, a guest or a teacher. The detail does the hardest part of starting a conversation for them, so neither person is left standing in silence.

blocks.name: et-intro

details: He just joined our chess club.
She taught me to play chess.

blocks.cap: The honored person’s name is said first.

blocks.title: Teacher and parent
blocks.q: At the school fair, Leo wants to introduce his mom to his teacher, Ms. Park. Whose name comes first?
steps: Both are adults. At school the teacher is something like the host, so many people say her name first; saying Mom’s name first is fine too.
Say one name first and present the other: “Ms. Park, this is my mom, Rosa Novak. Mom, this is Ms. Park, my science teacher.”
Add a detail: “She’s the one who helped with my volcano project.”
blocks.a: One good way: “Ms. Park, this is my mom, Rosa Novak. Mom, this is Ms. Park, my science teacher.”

blocks.title: Two friends
blocks.q: Ruby’s friend Sam and her cousin Hana are the same age. How does Ruby introduce them?
steps: With people your own age, either name can go first.
Say who each person is to you: “Sam, this is my cousin Hana. Hana, this is Sam from my class.”
Add a detail they share: “You both love drawing.”
blocks.a: “Sam, this is my cousin Hana. Hana, this is Sam from my class. You both love drawing.”

blocks.html: Saying the names in any order, or saying only the names and walking off. Check: did the older or honored person hear their name first, and did each person get a detail to start talking about?

Customs differ. The “older or honored person first” rule is the long-standing American and British custom. Families have their own ways, too. Whatever order you use, saying both names clearly and adding a detail is what makes an introduction kind.

blocks.html: When you introduce yourself to a grown-up, you also need to know what to call them. The custom in most of the U.S. is simple, and there is a polite way to handle the times you aren’t sure.

Use a title with the last name: Mr. Diaz, Ms. Park, Mrs. Hale, Dr. Bell. Use a first name only if the adult invites you to. When you aren’t sure whether a woman uses Mrs. or Ms., “Ms.” works for any woman.

A title shows respect for an adult’s age and role. Letting the adult decide whether to use first names puts the choice with them, so nobody is made uncomfortable. And when you follow what a person asks to be called, you show that you listened.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: “Good morning, Ms. Park.”
“Hey, Grace!” to your teacher.
cards.why: Use her title unless she asks you to use her first name.

cards.text: “Thank you, Dr. Bell.”
“Hey, you!” to a friend’s dad.
cards.why: Use his name with a title, or ask what to call him.

cards.text: “What should I call you?”
“Thanks, Priya,” after she asked you to call her Priya.

blocks.cap: Sort each greeting, then Check.

blocks.title: A friend’s parent
blocks.q: Sam meets his friend Omar’s mother for the first time. Omar’s last name is Haddad. What should Sam call her?
steps: Start with a title and the family’s last name: “Hello, Mrs. Haddad” or “Ms. Haddad.”
If she says, “Oh, please call me Layla,” then use Layla. If not, keep the title.
If Sam isn’t sure of her last name, he can ask Omar first.
blocks.a: “Hello, Ms. Haddad,” unless she invites him to use her first name.

blocks.title: Not sure
blocks.q: Mia’s new neighbor waves at her. Mia knows her name is Nora Grant but not whether she is married. What should Mia say?
steps: “Ms.” works for any woman, married or not.
“Hi, Ms. Grant!”
If Nora asks to be called something else, Mia can switch.
blocks.a: “Hi, Ms. Grant!”

blocks.html: Guessing wrong between Mrs. and Ms. and then avoiding the person’s name. “Ms.” works for any woman when you are not sure. And always follow what an adult asks to be called.

Customs differ. Customs differ by region and family. In parts of the South, children may say “Miss Ana” or “Mr. James” with a first name, and “sir” and “ma’am” are a common, respectful habit in many regions. Some families and schools use first names for adults. When in doubt, use the title and last name, and follow what the adult prefers.

blocks.html: Before you say a word, the way you stand already says something. Poise means looking calm, easy and ready to pay attention. It is not about looking stiff or perfect; it is about showing the people around you that you are present.
Stand tall and easy: weight on both feet, shoulders relaxed and back, head up, eyes forward, and hands still at your sides or lightly together in front.

People read your posture as a message. Slumping with your hands in your pockets can look as if you would rather be somewhere else, even when you don’t mean that. Standing easy and tall says, “I’m glad to be here, and I’m listening.” That is why poise is a courtesy: it is about how you make others feel.

blocks.title: Waiting to be called up
blocks.q: Mia is waiting on stage to receive a certificate. What does poise look like?
steps: Stand with weight on both feet, not leaning on one hip.
Head up, shoulders relaxed, hands still at her sides or lightly together.
Look toward the speaker; when her name is called, walk up at an easy pace.
blocks.a: Tall and easy, hands still, eyes on the speaker.

blocks.html: Standing stiff like a soldier, or slumping with your hands in your pockets. Poise looks relaxed, not rigid. Check yourself: can you breathe and smile easily? If you feel frozen, let your shoulders drop a little.

Poise is for everyone. People stand in many ways because bodies differ; some people use a wheelchair, a cane or crutches. Poise is the same idea for all of us: head up, attention on the people with you.

Customs differ. What looks respectful varies a little. In some cultures, standing with hands clasped in front or bowing the head slightly shows respect to elders. The idea underneath is the same everywhere: show people your attention.

blocks.html: Sitting well uses the same ideas as standing with poise: easy, upright and paying attention. You sit in class, at meals, in waiting rooms and at other people’s homes, so it is one of the habits people notice most.
Sit back in the chair, upright and relaxed, with your feet on the floor and your hands in your lap or resting on the table edge. Keep all four chair legs on the floor.

How you sit shows whether you are paying attention to the people with you. Sprawling across a couch or hanging over the back of a chair takes up space others might need and can look as if you are bored. Sitting well is a quiet way to say, “I’m with you.” Tipping a chair back is also hard on the chair and can startle people nearby.

blocks.title: At a friend’s house
blocks.q: Sam is visiting Omar’s family and sits on their couch while Omar’s grandmother talks to him. What does sitting well look like?
steps: Sit back on the couch, not sprawled across it.
Feet on the floor; shoes off the cushions.
Hands in his lap, and face her while she talks.
blocks.a: Sit back and upright, feet on the floor, hands still, facing her.

blocks.title: In class
blocks.q: Ruby is tired during the last class of the day. What can she do so she still looks attentive?
steps: Sit back in the chair with feet on the floor; avoid putting her head down on the desk.
Turn toward whoever is speaking.
Keep her hands still, not drumming or clicking a pen.
blocks.a: Sit back and upright, turned toward the speaker, hands still.

blocks.html: Sprawling, hanging an arm over the chair back, or tipping the chair onto two legs. A quick check: are all four chair legs and both your feet on the floor?

blocks.html: First impressions start at the door. Walking into a room uses standing with poise, plus one more thing: a greeting.
Walk in at an easy pace, look up, smile, and greet the people there, starting with the host or the adult in charge. If you are a guest, wait to be shown where to sit, or ask.

A greeting at the door lets people know you are glad to be there and that you see them. Sliding in with your eyes on your phone can look as if the room doesn’t matter to you. Waiting to be shown a seat respects the host, who may have a plan, like saving a chair for someone.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: Walking into a friend’s birthday party
items: Put your phone away before you go in.
Walk in at an easy pace and look up.
Smile and greet the host’s parent: “Hi, Ms. Lopez!”
Find your friend and say, “Happy birthday!”
Ask where to put the gift, or wait to be shown.

blocks.title: Arriving at a family dinner
blocks.q: Leo arrives at his aunt’s house for dinner. Several relatives are already in the living room. What should he do?
steps: Put his phone away and walk in looking up.
Greet his aunt, the host, first: “Hi, Aunt Rosa, thanks for having us.”
Then say hello to the others, especially grandparents, and wait to be told where to sit at the table.
blocks.a: Greet the host first, then the others, and wait to be shown a seat.

blocks.title: Arriving late
blocks.q: Hana’s club meeting has already started when she arrives. How can she enter politely?
steps: Come in quietly, without letting the door bang.
Give a small smile or wave to the leader instead of talking over the meeting.
Take the nearest open seat, and apologize briefly afterward: “Sorry I was late.”
blocks.a: Come in quietly, a small wave to the leader, nearest seat, a short apology afterward.

blocks.html: Slipping in while looking at your phone, or heading straight for a seat without a word. Check: did you look up and greet someone at the door?

blocks.html: You know how to sit well. Here is when to stand up instead. Standing to greet is one of the oldest and simplest signs of respect, and it still makes a strong impression.
Stand up when an adult or a guest enters the room or comes over to meet you, and whenever you are introduced. Then greet them, and sit again once they have settled or invite you to.

Getting up takes a little effort, and that is the point: standing says, “You matter enough for me to get up.” It also puts you face to face, which makes a greeting or a handshake easier. Staying on the couch and waving can look as if the screen or the game matters more.

choices.text: Put the phone down, stand up, and say, “Hi, Grandpa! It’s great to see you.”
choices.outcome: Grandpa feels welcomed. Standing up says he matters.

choices.text: Wave from the couch and keep scrolling.
choices.outcome: Grandpa feels less important than the phone.

choices.text: Say “Hi” without looking up.
choices.outcome: A greeting is good, but Grandpa can’t see Omar’s face. Stand and look up.

blocks.title: A teacher stops by
blocks.q: Ms. Park comes over to the lunch table to talk to Ruby’s mom at the school picnic. Ruby is sitting. What should she do?
steps: Stand up as Ms. Park arrives.
Greet her: “Hi, Ms. Park.”
Sit down again once the grown-ups are talking or Ms. Park says, “Please, sit.”
blocks.a: Stand, greet her, and sit again when it is natural.

blocks.title: Being introduced
blocks.q: At a family party, Sam’s dad brings a friend over: “Sam, this is Mr. Reed.” Sam is sitting on the steps. What should he do?
steps: Stand up for the introduction.
Shake hands if Mr. Reed offers his hand, and say, “Nice to meet you, Mr. Reed.”
Sit back down when they move on.
blocks.a: Stand up, shake hands, and say, “Nice to meet you, Mr. Reed.”

blocks.html: Staying seated and waving from the couch. Check: when someone new walks over, are you on your feet for the greeting?
If standing is hard for you, because of an injury or a disability, a warm greeting, a smile and looking up are the same courtesy. Etiquette asks for respect, not for everyone to do it the same way.

blocks.html: Setting the table is one of the most useful jobs you can do at home, and the pattern is the same in nearly every American home and restaurant. Once you learn it, you will never have to wonder where the fork goes.
Fork on the left. Knife on the right, with the blade facing the plate. Spoon to the right of the knife. Glass above the knife. Napkin on the left, beside the fork (or under it).

The pattern follows the hands. Most people cut with the right hand, so the knife sits on the right; the fork is picked up with the left. The blade faces the plate so nobody reaches past a sharp edge. And because everyone sets the table the same way, guests always know which glass is theirs: the one on their right.

blocks.name: et-setting
blocks.cap: Drag or tap each piece to its spot, then Check.

blocks.title: Setting one place
blocks.q: Ruby is setting the table for spaghetti. Each person gets a plate, a fork, a knife, a spoon, a glass and a napkin. Where does each go?
steps: Plate in the middle, in front of the chair.
Fork on the left; the folded napkin to the left of the fork.
Knife on the right, blade toward the plate; spoon to the right of the knife.
Glass above the tip of the knife.
blocks.a: Napkin, fork, plate, knife (blade in), spoon, with the glass above the knife.

blocks.title: A memory trick
blocks.q: Leo can never remember which side the fork goes on. What trick can help?
steps: Count the letters: “fork” and “left” both have four.
“Knife,” “spoon” and “right” all have five.
So the fork goes left; the knife and spoon go right.
blocks.a: Fork and left have four letters; knife, spoon and right have five.

blocks.html: Putting the fork and knife on the same side, or turning the knife blade outward. Check with the letter trick, and look at the knife: the sharp edge should point at the plate.
Setting for more courses? Utensils go in the order you will use them, from the outside in, and a bread plate goes at the upper left. That is the next step, in the Teens and Adults course.

blocks.html: Now that you can set the table, here is how to use what is on it. Americans hold the fork and knife in two ways, and both are correct.

To cut, hold the fork in your left hand, tines down, and the knife in your right, with your index finger along the back of the blade. Cut one or two bites at a time. In the American style, you then set the knife on the edge of the plate and switch the fork to your right hand to eat. In the Continental style, the fork stays in your left hand and the knife stays in your right.

Cutting a bite or two at a time keeps your food warm and the meal calm. A finger along the back of the knife gives you control, so you cut gently instead of sawing. Both styles are tidy and quiet, which is what matters.

items: Hold the fork in your left hand, tines down, to keep the food still.
Hold the knife in your right hand, index finger along the back.
Cut one bite with a few gentle strokes.
Set the knife across the top edge of your plate.
Move the fork to your right hand and eat the bite.

blocks.title: Cutting chicken
blocks.q: Omar has a piece of chicken. How should he cut it?
steps: Fork in his left hand, tines down, holding the chicken still; knife in his right, finger along the back.
Cut one bite, eat it, then cut the next.
blocks.a: One bite at a time, fork left and knife right while cutting.

blocks.title: A guest who eats differently
blocks.q: At dinner, Hana notices her cousin’s friend keeps the fork in her left hand the whole meal. Is that a mistake?
steps: No. That is the Continental style, used across Europe and by many Americans.
Both styles are correct in the U.S.
There is nothing to correct or comment on.
blocks.a: No. It is the Continental style, and it is correct.

blocks.html: Holding the knife like a dagger in a fist, or cutting the whole plate of food at once. Hold it with your finger along the back and cut one or two bites at a time.
Customs differ. Some families eat certain dishes with chopsticks, bread or their hands. Each way is correct in its place.

blocks.html: At a family-style meal, dishes go around the table instead of being served from the kitchen. Once you know where everything sits, passing is the next skill, and a few simple customs keep it from turning into a scramble.

Pass dishes to the right (counterclockwise). If you start a dish, offer it to your neighbor or hold it while they serve themselves. Pass the salt and pepper together, even if someone asks for only one. When someone asks for a dish, pass it to them without helping yourself on the way.

When every dish travels the same direction, no two bowls collide and nobody gets skipped. The salt and pepper travel as a pair so nobody has to hunt for the other one. And handing a dish straight to the person who asked respects their turn.

say: Could you please pass the salt?
opts.prompt: Leo has the salt and the pepper. What should he do?

choices.text: Pass the salt and the pepper together.
choices.outcome: The pair stays together, so the next person doesn’t have to hunt for the pepper.

choices.text: Shake some salt on his own food first, then pass it.
choices.outcome: Sam asked first. Pass it straight to him, and ask for it back later.

choices.text: Slide the salt across the table to Sam.
choices.outcome: Sliding can tip things over. Hand it along, and send the pepper too.

blocks.cap: Choose what Leo does.

blocks.title: Starting the potatoes
blocks.q: The mashed potatoes are in front of Mia. Everyone is ready to start. What should she do?
steps: Offer them first: hold the bowl for the person on her left, or ask, “Would you like some?”
Serve herself a fair share.
Pass the bowl to the right.
blocks.a: Offer, serve herself, then pass to the right.

blocks.title: Passing to someone far away
blocks.q: At the other end of the table, Grandpa Walt asks for the rolls. Ruby is holding the basket. What should she do?
steps: Pass the basket toward Grandpa through the people in between, the shortest way.
Don’t take a roll on the way; he asked first.
If she wants one, she can ask for the basket back afterward.
blocks.a: Pass it along to Grandpa without taking one, and ask for it later.

blocks.html: Taking a dish that was passed to someone else, or sending the salt without the pepper. Check: is the dish going to the person who asked? Are the salt and pepper traveling as a pair?
Pass bowls with the handle or the serving spoon turned toward the person taking it, and hold a hot dish with a napkin or pot holder.

blocks.html: When a dish is passed to you, you serve yourself. A few habits make sure there is enough for everyone and that the food stays clean for the next person.

Use the serving spoon, not your own fork. Take a fair share, so everyone gets some; seconds can come later. Put the serving spoon back in the dish. Then wait to eat until everyone has been served and the host or cook begins.

The serving spoon keeps the shared food clean: your own fork has been in your mouth. A fair share is kindness to the people after you; the last person to get the dish should still have some. Waiting until everyone is served means nobody eats alone while others are still filling their plates.

cards.text: Using the serving spoon for the beans.
Spearing a meatball with your own fork from the bowl.
cards.why: Use the serving spoon so the shared food stays clean.

cards.text: Taking a fair share so the dish goes all the way around.
Taking half the lasagna because it is your favorite.
cards.why: Take a fair share first; ask for seconds later.

cards.text: Putting the serving spoon back in the dish.
Starting to eat while Grandma is still serving herself.

blocks.title: A favorite dish
blocks.q: Sam loves enchiladas. There are eight enchiladas and six people. How many should Sam take on the first pass?
steps: Count: eight enchiladas, six people.
A fair share is one each, which leaves two extra.
Take one, and ask later, “May I have another, if there are extras?”
blocks.a: One, and ask for a second one after everyone has been served.

blocks.title: A food you don’t like
blocks.q: The green beans come to Hana, and she doesn’t like them. What can she do?
steps: She can say, “No, thank you,” and pass the dish on.
Many families ask children to take a small taste; follow your family’s custom.
She should not say “Yuck” or make a face; someone worked to make it.
blocks.a: “No, thank you,” pass it along, or take a small taste if that is the family custom.

blocks.html: Taking a huge first helping of a favorite dish before everyone has some. Count the people and take a fair share; seconds come later.

Customs differ. Families start meals in different ways. Some wait for the cook to sit down, some for the host to pick up a fork, and some say a blessing or a few words first. Follow the family you are with. If you are a guest, watch the host.

blocks.html: You already know how to sit well and how to pass dishes. Two more habits keep a meal pleasant for the people beside you: asking instead of reaching, and keeping your space tidy.
If something is out of easy reach, ask: “Could you please pass the butter?” Keep your elbows off the table while you are eating. Keep phones, toys and hats away from the table.

Reaching across someone puts your arm in front of their face and over their plate, and it can knock over a glass. Asking takes two seconds and gives the other person a chance to help. Elbows on the table while eating crowd your neighbors and lean you over your plate. And a phone or a toy at the table tells the people there that something else matters more.

blocks.cap: Tap the figure who is sitting well at the table, then Check.

blocks.title: The butter is far away
blocks.q: The butter is in front of Grandpa Walt, two seats from Omar. What should Omar do?
steps: Ask the person closest to it: “Grandpa, could you please pass the butter?”
Wait for it to come to him.
Say thank you when it arrives.
blocks.a: “Grandpa, could you please pass the butter?” and “Thank you.”

blocks.title: Between courses
blocks.q: Dinner is over and everyone is talking, waiting for dessert. Ruby rests her forearms on the table. Is that rude?
steps: Most etiquette writers say elbows are fine between courses or after the meal, while people are talking and not eating.
The custom is about not leaning over your food while eating.
Some families prefer elbows off at all times, so follow your family’s rule.
blocks.a: Usually not. Elbows are generally fine between courses; follow the family’s custom.

blocks.html: Thinking elbows are never allowed. Most etiquette writers say elbows on the table are fine between courses or after the meal, just not while you are eating. The bigger rule is about not crowding or reaching over your neighbors.

Customs differ. Hats and caps come off at the table in most American homes; religious head coverings stay on. In some families phones are fine at a casual meal, and in others they are never allowed. When you are a guest, follow the house custom, and when in doubt, put the phone away.

blocks.html: Everyone drops a fork sooner or later, even grown-ups at fancy dinners. Knowing how a meal works helps, but the real skill is staying calm when something goes a little wrong.

Quiet and quick is the rule. At home, pick up a dropped fork and get a clean one. At a restaurant, leave it and quietly ask the server for another. For a small spill, say “Excuse me,” wipe it with your napkin, and help clean up.

A mishap is only a big deal if someone makes it one. Handling it quietly keeps the meal pleasant for everyone and saves you from embarrassment. A fork that has been on the floor is dirty, so you get a clean one rather than wiping it and using it again.

Wiping a dropped fork on your napkin and using it.

Pointing out a spill someone else made.

steps: Say “Excuse me” or “Sorry about that.”
Set the glass upright and blot the spill with his napkin.
If it is a big spill, tell the host and offer to help clean it, then carry on with the meal.
blocks.a: “Excuse me,” blot it, offer to help, and carry on.

blocks.title: Someone else’s mishap
blocks.q: Grandma June drops her spoon on the floor. What can Mia do?
steps: Don’t make a fuss or point it out.
Offer quietly: “I’ll get you a clean one, Grandma.”
Bring a clean spoon and sit back down.
blocks.a: Quietly get her a clean spoon.

blocks.html: Making a big fuss, or wiping a dropped fork on a napkin and using it again. Quiet and quick is the rule, and a fork that touched the floor needs to be replaced.

Other small mishaps: if you burp, say “Excuse me” quietly. If you need to cough or sneeze, turn away from the table and use your elbow or a tissue. If a bite has a pit or a bit of bone, take it out the way it went in, with your fork or fingers, and set it on the edge of your plate.

blocks.html: After you serve yourself and enjoy the meal, one more habit finishes it well. Someone planned, shopped and cooked so you could eat. A thank-you tells them their work was noticed.

Thank whoever cooked and say something kind and specific about the meal: “Thank you for dinner. The bread was great.” Then offer to help clear the table, and ask to be excused if you need to leave before others.

Thanks are for the work, not just for food you loved. Even on a night when you didn’t like a dish, the cook spent time and care on everyone. A specific detail shows you noticed, and offering to help turns thanks into action.

blocks.title: Dinner at a friend’s house
blocks.q: Sam eats dinner at Ruby’s house. Ruby’s mom made tacos. What should he say at the end?
steps: Thank the cook by name: “Thank you for dinner, Ms. Walsh.”
Add something specific: “The tacos were delicious.”
Offer to help: “Can I help clear the plates?”

blocks.title: Leaving the table early
blocks.q: Omar has to get ready for practice before the others finish. What should he do?
steps: Thank the cook first.
Ask to be excused: “May I please be excused? I need to get ready for practice.”
Take his plate to the kitchen if that is the family custom.
blocks.a: “Thanks for dinner, Mom. May I please be excused?”

blocks.html: Thanking the cook only when you liked the food. Thank them for the work, and find something true and kind to say: the bread, the table, the effort, or simply “Thank you for making dinner.”

blocks.html: Texting is quick, but some things go better with a call: talking to a grandparent, asking a coach a question, or calling a friend’s house when a parent may answer. A good phone call has a simple shape, and the other person can’t see you, so your words do all the work.
Greet the person, say who you are, ask if it is a good time, say why you are calling, and say goodbye before you hang up. “Hi, this is Ruby, Hana’s friend. Is Hana there, please?”

On the phone, the other person can’t see who is talking, so saying your name right away saves them from guessing. Asking whether it is a good time respects their day: they may be cooking, driving or about to leave. A clear reason and a goodbye make the call easy to follow and easy to end.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: Calling a friend’s house
items: Say hello when someone answers.
Say who you are: “This is Ruby, Hana’s friend.”
Ask for your friend: “Is Hana there, please?”
When Hana comes on, ask, “Is this a good time?”
Say why you called.
Say goodbye before you hang up.

blocks.title: Calling Grandma
blocks.q: Leo wants to call Grandma June to thank her for a birthday card. How might the call go?
steps: Greet and say who it is, even with family; her phone may not show the name: “Hi, Grandma, it’s Leo.”
Ask if it’s a good time: “Is this a good time to talk?”
Say why he called: “I wanted to thank you for the card.” Then chat, and say goodbye: “Love you, bye!”
blocks.a: “Hi, Grandma, it’s Leo. Is this a good time? I wanted to thank you for the card.”

blocks.title: Calling the coach
blocks.q: Omar needs to tell Coach Diaz he will miss practice. What should he say?
steps: Greet and give his full name: “Hi, Coach Diaz, this is Omar Haddad from the team.”
Ask if it is a good time.
Give the reason clearly and briefly: “I have a dentist appointment Thursday, so I’ll miss practice.” Then thank him and say goodbye.
blocks.a: “Hi, Coach Diaz, this is Omar Haddad. Is this a good time? I’ll miss Thursday’s practice because of a dentist appointment. Thanks, bye.”

blocks.html: Starting to talk without saying your name, or calling during dinner or late at night. Check: did you say who you are in your first sentence? Is it a reasonable hour for the family you are calling?
If you reach voicemail, leave a short message: your name, why you called, your number and a goodbye. Speak slowly when you say the number.

blocks.html: You know how to make a call. Answering the family phone, or a parent’s phone when they ask you to, is the other half. It is a real job: a message is only helpful if it reaches the person it is for.

Answer with a greeting. If the call is for someone else, ask, “May I tell them who’s calling?” If they can’t come to the phone, write down the caller’s name, number and message, and the time, and give it to the person.

A calm greeting makes the caller feel welcome. Asking who is calling, instead of shouting “WHO IS THIS?”, is polite and lets the person decide whether to come to the phone. Writing the message down matters because memories slip, and a lost message can mean a missed appointment or a friend left waiting.

blocks.name: et-note

parts.message: Your appointment moved to Friday at 3:00. Please call back to confirm.

blocks.cap: A complete phone message: who it is for, who called, the number, the message, the time and who took it.

blocks.title: A call for Dad
blocks.q: The family phone rings, and Mia answers. The caller asks for her dad, who is in the yard. What should she say?
steps: Greet: “Hello, this is the Brooks house, Mia speaking.” Or simply “Hello?”, as her family prefers.
Ask: “May I tell him who’s calling?”
Say, “Please hold on, I’ll get him,” set the phone down gently, and go get him instead of shouting across the house.
blocks.a: “May I tell him who’s calling? Please hold on, I’ll get him.”

blocks.title: Taking a message
blocks.q: Ms. Park calls for Sam’s mom, who is out. What should Sam write down?
steps: Who the message is for: Mom.
Who called and her number: Ms. Park, and the number she gives, read back to check it.
The message, the time, and his own name, then put it where Mom will see it.
blocks.a: For Mom; from Ms. Park; her number; the message; the time; taken by Sam.

blocks.html: Shouting across the house for the person, or forgetting to write the message down. Go get them, and if they can’t come, write it down right away and read the number back to the caller.
If a caller you don’t know asks questions you aren’t sure about, it is fine to say, “Please hold on,” and get a grown-up. You never have to answer questions that make you uncomfortable.

blocks.html: Video calls are phone calls with a picture, for a class, a club, or a chat with family far away. Because people can see you, a few more courtesies come in.
Find a quiet spot with light on your face (a window or lamp in front of you, not behind). Look at the camera when you talk, mute when you aren’t talking, and give the call your attention.

Treat a video call like sitting across a table from someone. Noise, a dark screen or a bouncing camera make it hard for others to follow, and an open microphone sends every crunch and barking dog to everyone. Looking at the camera is how you “look at” people on a screen, and paying attention shows them their time matters.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Muting your microphone while others talk.
Eating chips with the microphone on.
cards.why: Every crunch goes to everyone. Mute, or eat later.

cards.text: Sitting with a window in front of you.
Walking around the house with the camera bouncing.
cards.why: Sit still somewhere, the way you would at a table.

cards.text: Looking at the camera when you talk.
Playing a game in another window during class.
cards.why: Give the call your attention.

blocks.title: A class on video
blocks.q: Hana has a class on video. Her little brother is playing loudly nearby. What can she do?
steps: Move to a quieter room if she can, or close the door.
Mute her microphone until she needs to talk.
When the teacher calls on her, unmute, look at the camera and speak clearly.
blocks.a: Quiet spot, mute until she speaks, then unmute and look at the camera.

blocks.title: A call with Grandpa
blocks.q: Sam is video-chatting with Grandpa Walt, but Sam’s screen shows only a dark shape. Why, and how can he fix it?
steps: The window is behind him, so the camera sees bright light and his face looks dark.
Turn around so the window or a lamp lights his face.
Hold the device steady or set it on a table at eye level.
blocks.a: The light is behind him; face the window or lamp and keep the camera steady.

blocks.html: Leaving the microphone on while you eat, or walking around with the camera bouncing. Before you join: quiet spot, light in front, device steady, microphone ready to mute.
Join a scheduled call on time, dressed as you would be for that class or meeting, and say hello and goodbye, just as you would in person.

blocks.html: A text is like a phone call with no voice. That makes it fast, but it also takes away the smile and the tone that tell people what you mean.
Text at reasonable hours, write clearly, and read your message before you send it. Remember that tone is hard to hear in text, so add a friendly word or two.

In person, a smile shows when you are joking. In a text, the same words can sound cold or angry. A one-letter “k” can read as “I’m annoyed,” even if you were only busy. Reading before you send catches words that might hurt, and texting at reasonable hours respects the fact that the buzz can wake someone up.

blocks.name: et-text

choices.text: k
choices.why: A one-letter answer can read as cold. Aunt Rosa wants to know you liked it.

choices.text: Yes! Thank you so much for the art kit. I already painted a bird!
choices.why: Warm, specific and quick. That is a great reply.

choices.text: YES IT CAME
choices.why: All capital letters read like shouting, and there is no thank-you.

blocks.cap: Choose a reply and read the note.

blocks.title: A late-night idea
blocks.q: At 10:45 p.m., Leo remembers something funny he wants to tell Omar. What should he do?
steps: It is late; the buzz could wake Omar or his family.
Save it as a draft or write it down.
Send it in the morning.
blocks.a: Wait until morning to send it.

blocks.title: Fixing a curt text
blocks.q: Mia’s friend asks, “Want to come over Saturday?” Mia can’t. Her first draft says, “No.” How can she make it kinder?
steps: “No.” alone can sound like she doesn’t want to see her friend.
Add a thank-you and a reason or a wish: “Thanks for asking! I have a game Saturday.”
Offer another time if she can: “Could we do Sunday?”
blocks.a: “Thanks for asking! I have a game Saturday. Could we do Sunday?”

blocks.html: Sending a curt “k” or “fine” that reads as annoyed, or texting late at night. A short friendly word or two prevents a lot of hurt feelings. Check before sending: would this sound kind if someone read it in a grumpy voice?
Customs differ. Families set different rules about phones and texting hours. Follow yours, and for other families, assume early evening is fine and late at night is not.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: A group chat is texting with an audience. Everything you send is seen by everyone in it, and it can be copied, saved and shared, so group chats need a little extra care.

Stay on topic, don’t share screenshots or private messages without asking, and never use a chat to leave someone out or gang up on anyone. If a chat turns mean, don’t join in, and tell a trusted grown-up if it keeps going.

A message sent to one friend was meant for that friend. Sharing it with a group breaks their trust, even if the words were already “sent.” Teasing in a group stings more, because everyone sees it. And making a new chat to talk about someone who was left out of it is a modern way of whispering behind their back.

blocks.name: et-text

opts.title: Soccer team

messages.text: Hana kicks like a baby lol
Can someone give me a ride?

opts.why: Teasing someone in front of the whole group hurts more, and the message can be copied and shared.

blocks.cap: Tap the message that is unkind, then Check.

blocks.title: A screenshot
blocks.q: Sam’s friend sent him a private message about being nervous for the tryouts. Another friend says, “Screenshot it to the group, it’s funny.” What should Sam do?
steps: The message was meant only for Sam.
Sharing it would embarrass his friend and break his trust.
Say no: “Nah, that was just to me.”
blocks.a: Don’t share it. Private messages stay private unless the sender says it’s okay.

blocks.title: A side chat
blocks.q: Mia sees that some classmates made a new chat called “Everyone but Ruby.” What can she do?
steps: Don’t join in or add anything unkind.
She can leave the chat or say, “This isn’t cool.”
If it keeps going or gets mean, tell a trusted grown-up. Being kind to Ruby in person helps too.
blocks.a: Don’t join in, speak up or leave, and tell a trusted grown-up if it continues.

blocks.html: Thinking a screenshot is harmless because the words were already sent. Sharing someone’s message with others breaks their trust. Ask first, every time.
Other group-chat courtesies: keep late-night messages to a minimum, don’t flood the chat with dozens of stickers, and if a chat is for one purpose, like a team schedule, keep it to that.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: You know about texting and group chats. The last phone habit may be the most important one: knowing when to put it down.

When someone is talking with you, put the phone down. At meals, visits and conversations, the people in front of you come first. If you must check something, say so: “Sorry, my mom’s texting about pickup. One second.”

Looking at a phone while someone talks tells them, without a word, that the screen is more interesting than they are. People notice, even when you think you are being sneaky. Putting the phone away is one of the simplest ways to show someone they matter.

blocks.name: et-scene

say: Ruby, tell me about your science fair project!
opts.prompt: Grandma June asks Ruby a question while Ruby is looking at her phone. What should Ruby do?

choices.text: Put the phone face down and answer: “It’s about bees! Want to hear?”
choices.outcome: Grandma feels that Ruby wants to talk with her.

choices.text: Keep scrolling and say, “Uh-huh, it’s good.”
choices.outcome: Grandma can tell the phone has Ruby’s attention, not her.

choices.text: Text under the table while answering.
choices.outcome: Everyone notices texting under the table. Put it away.

blocks.cap: Choose what Ruby does.

blocks.title: Waiting for an important message
blocks.q: Omar is at dinner with his friend’s family, but his mom said she would text about pickup time. What should he do?
steps: Keep the phone in his pocket, on silent or vibrate.
If it buzzes, say, “Excuse me, that’s probably my mom about pickup,” and check it quickly.
Reply briefly, put it away, and rejoin the conversation.
blocks.a: Mention it, check quickly when it buzzes, then put it away.

blocks.title: With friends
blocks.q: Sam and Leo are hanging out, and Leo keeps scrolling while Sam talks. What could Sam say, kindly?
steps: Assume the best; Leo may not realize it.
Say it lightly: “Hey, want to put the phones away and play a game?”
And Leo can do the polite thing: put it away and say sorry.
blocks.a: “Hey, want to put the phones away and play a game?”

blocks.html: Texting “under the table” and thinking no one notices. Everyone notices, and it tells them they are less interesting than the screen. Put the phone away, or say why you need to look.

Customs differ. Families have different rules about phones at casual meals. Some are fine with a quick check; many say none at the table at all. At someone else’s home, follow their rule, and when in doubt, keep it in your pocket.

blocks.html: When a friend comes to your house, you become the host. That is a real job, and a fun one. A good host makes a guest feel welcome from the moment they arrive.
Greet your friend and the parent who drops them off, offer a snack or a drink, give a choice of what to do, and include everyone who is there, including brothers, sisters and other friends.

Being a guest in someone else’s home can feel a little strange: different rules, different rooms, people you don’t know. A good host takes that feeling away. Offering choices puts your friend’s fun first, and including everyone means nobody spends the afternoon feeling left out.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.prompt: Sam and his dad arrive at Leo’s door. What should Leo do first?

choices.text: “Hi, Sam! Hi, Mr. Rivera! Come on in. Want a snack before we play?”
choices.outcome: Leo greeted both of them and offered a snack. Sam feels welcome.

choices.text: “Come see my new game!” and runs off without a word to Sam’s dad.
choices.outcome: Sam’s dad was left at the door. Greet the parent too.

choices.text: Lets them in and goes back to his video.
choices.outcome: Sam came to play with Leo. The guest’s good time is the host’s job.

blocks.cap: Choose what Leo does.

blocks.title: Choosing what to do
blocks.q: Ruby has her friend Mia over. Ruby wants to play her favorite video game, but Mia isn’t into games. What should Ruby do?
steps: A host puts the guest’s fun first.
Offer two or three choices: “Do you want to bake cookies, play outside or do a puzzle?”
Go with what Mia picks; Ruby can play her game another time.
blocks.a: “Do you want to bake, play outside or do a puzzle?” and go with Mia’s pick.

blocks.title: A little sister
blocks.q: Omar’s friend is over, and his little sister keeps asking to join. What can Omar do?
steps: Find something everyone can do together for part of the time, like a card game.
If the friends want time alone later, say it kindly: “We’ll play with you after our game.”
Ask a parent for help if needed, instead of shooing her away rudely.
blocks.a: Include her in a game for a while, and be kind when they want time alone.

blocks.html: Playing a game only you enjoy, or leaving a sibling or a second friend out. Check: has your guest had a say in what you do? Is anyone sitting alone?
When your friend leaves, walk them to the door, say “Thanks for coming,” and say goodbye to their parent too.

blocks.html: A sleepover is a longer visit, so the guest manners you already know matter even more. This time you are the guest, in another family’s home overnight.

At a sleepover, follow the family’s rules and bedtime, offer to help, keep your things tidy, and thank the parents in the morning. And remember: it is always fine to call home if you feel uncomfortable or want to leave.

Each home has its own rules, and as a guest you live by theirs for the night. Following them shows respect for the family who invited you. Offering to help and keeping your things tidy say thank you before you even say it. And knowing you can call home lets you relax and enjoy the night.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Going to sleep when the parents ask for lights out.
Staying up loudly after the parents asked for quiet.
cards.why: Their house, their bedtime.

cards.text: Asking before taking a snack from the kitchen.
Leaving your sleeping bag and clothes all over the floor.
cards.why: Keep your things together and roll up your bag in the morning.

cards.text: Saying, “Thank you for having me,” in the morning.
Complaining that breakfast isn’t what you eat at home.
cards.why: Try what is offered, or say “No, thank you.”

blocks.cap: Sort each habit as polite or rude, then Check.

blocks.title: A different rule
blocks.q: At Hana’s house, everyone takes their shoes off at the door, and there are no phones after nine o’clock. Ruby’s family doesn’t do either. What should Ruby do?
steps: Follow Hana’s family’s rules while she is their guest.
Take her shoes off at the door and put her phone away at nine.
There is no need to say how her family does it differently.
blocks.a: Shoes off and phone away at nine, just as Hana’s family does.

blocks.title: Wanting to go home
blocks.q: At a sleepover, Sam starts to feel homesick and uneasy. What can he do?
steps: It is fine to call home. He can tell his friend’s parent, “I’d like to call my mom.”
He does not need to explain more than he wants to.
In the morning, or when he leaves, he can still thank the family: “Thank you for having me.”
blocks.a: Ask the friend’s parent to help him call home. That is always okay.

blocks.html: Staying up after the parents asked for quiet, or helping yourself to snacks without asking. As a guest, follow their rules and ask first. And if anything feels wrong, it is fine to say no and call home.

Customs differ. Families differ: some take shoes off at the door, some say a few words before meals, some have early bedtimes. Respect every way, follow the house you are in, and never make fun of how another family does things.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: Birthday parties start with invitations, and invitations come with jobs for both the host and the guests. Like having a friend over, the goal is that everyone feels welcome, including people who aren’t coming.
When you get an invitation, reply by the date it asks: “RSVP” means please reply. When you are the host, don’t hand out invitations or talk about the party in front of people who were not invited.

A host needs to know how many people are coming to plan food, seats and games. Replying, yes or no, is a kindness to them. “RSVP” comes from the French répondez s’il vous plaît, “please reply.” And because not everyone can be invited to every party, keeping invitations private spares feelings.

blocks.name: et-note

parts.attire: Play clothes; we’ll have a water-balloon toss!
parts.rsvp: RSVP to Omar’s mom by May 2: 555-0186

blocks.cap: An invitation names the host, the occasion, the time and place, what to wear and how to reply.

blocks.title: Replying
blocks.q: Leo gets the invitation above. He can come. What should he do, and by when?
steps: Find the reply line: RSVP to Omar’s mom by May 2.
Have a parent help him call or text her before May 2.
Say yes clearly and thank her: “Leo would love to come. Thank you for inviting him!”
blocks.a: Reply to Omar’s mom by May 2: “Leo would love to come. Thank you!”

blocks.title: Can’t come
blocks.q: Mia is invited to Hana’s party but has a family trip that day. Does she need to reply?
steps: Yes. “RSVP” asks for a reply either way.
Reply by the date: “Thank you so much for inviting me. I’m sorry I can’t come; we’ll be away. I hope it’s a great party!”
She can wish Hana a happy birthday at school.
blocks.a: Yes. Reply by the date with thanks and regrets.

blocks.html: Never replying, or saying yes and then not showing up. The host is counting on your answer. If your plans change after you reply, tell the host as soon as you can.
Hosting? Invite either the whole class or a small group quietly, by mail, by a parent’s text, or in person away from the others. At the party, talk about it only with the guests.

blocks.html: Many parties and holidays come with gifts. A gift doesn’t have to be expensive to be a good one. The best gifts show you thought about the other person.
Choose a gift with the person in mind, take the price tag off, add a card with your name, and let them open it when they like. Never say how much it cost.

A gift is a way of saying, “I know you, and I thought about you.” That is why the thought matters more than the price. Removing the price tag keeps the focus on the gift and away from money, and a card makes sure the person knows whom to thank.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: A sketchbook for a friend who loves drawing.
The game you want, so you can play it at their house.
cards.why: Choose for them, not for you.

cards.text: Taking the price sticker off before wrapping.
“This cost forty dollars, so you’d better like it.”
cards.why: Price talk makes a gift about money.

cards.text: A card that says who it’s from.
A homemade card and cookies for Grandma.

blocks.cap: Sort each gift idea, then Check.

blocks.title: Choosing a gift
blocks.q: Sam needs a birthday gift for Ruby. He knows she loves birds, and he has a small budget. What could he choose?
steps: Think about Ruby: what does she enjoy?
Find something that fits her interest and his budget: a small book about birds, a bird-shaped bookmark, or seeds for a feeder.
Take off the price tag and add a card: “Happy birthday, Ruby! From Sam.”
blocks.a: A small bird-themed gift, price tag off, with a card from Sam.

blocks.title: A homemade gift
blocks.q: Hana wants to give her grandfather something, but she has no money. Is a homemade gift okay?
steps: Yes. A gift is about the thought.
A drawing, a letter, a batch of cookies or a promise to help in his garden all show care.
Wrap it or put it in an envelope, with a note saying it is from her.
blocks.a: Yes. A homemade gift shows real thought.

blocks.html: Choosing the gift you would want, or saying how much it cost. Check: does this gift fit what the other person likes? Is the price tag off?

Customs differ. Customs differ about when gifts are opened. In many American families, gifts are opened at the party; in some families and cultures, gifts are opened later, privately. Both are polite, so let the person decide.

blocks.html: Now turn it around. When someone gives you a gift, how you receive it matters just as much. The giver is watching your face, hoping you’ll be pleased.
Read the card first, look at the giver, thank them warmly, and say something kind, even if you already have one or it isn’t your style.

A gift is a thought from another person, so you thank them for thinking of you, whatever is in the box. Reading the card first tells you whom to thank. A warm, kind response makes the giver glad they chose it; a disappointed face or “I already have this” can hurt for a long time.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.prompt: Grandpa Walt gives Mia a sweater. She already has one just like it. What should she say?

choices.text: “Thank you, Grandpa! It’s so soft. I love this color.”
choices.outcome: Mia thanked him for the thought and said something kind and true.

choices.text: “I already have this one.”
choices.outcome: True, but it hurts. Thank him for thinking of her; questions about exchanging can come later, privately.

choices.text: “Do you have the receipt?”
choices.outcome: Asking about returns in front of the giver makes the gift about the store, not the thought.

blocks.cap: Choose what Mia says.

blocks.title: A gift you don’t love
blocks.q: Leo’s aunt gives him a puzzle with a thousand pieces. Leo doesn’t like puzzles. What should he say?
steps: Thank her for the thought: “Thank you, Aunt Rosa!”
Find something kind and true: “This picture is really cool,” or “Maybe we can do it together at the holidays.”
Don’t say he doesn’t like puzzles.
blocks.a: “Thank you, Aunt Rosa! The picture is really cool.”

blocks.title: Opening several gifts
blocks.q: At her party, Ruby opens gifts from six friends. How can she make each giver feel thanked?
steps: Read each card first, so she knows who gave which gift.
Look at that friend and thank them by name: “Thanks, Omar! I love it.”
Don’t compare gifts or rush past one to get to the next.
blocks.a: Card first, then a warm thank-you by name for each gift.

blocks.html: Saying “I already have this” or “Do you have the receipt?” in front of the giver. Thank them for thinking of you; any question about exchanging comes later, privately, if at all.
Customs differ. In some families and cultures, gifts are set aside and opened later, not in front of the giver. In others, gifts are opened right away. Follow the custom of the people you are with.

blocks.html: After you receive a gift, a thank-you note finishes the job. It takes about five minutes, and it may be kept for years.
A thank-you note has a greeting, a thank-you for the specific gift or kindness, a line about how you will use or enjoy it, a warm closing and your signature. Send it within a week or two.

A note shows that you took time to thank someone, just as they took time to choose a gift for you. Naming the gift proves you noticed what they chose, and a detail about using it lets them picture you enjoying it. That is what makes a giver feel thanked.

blocks.name: et-note

parts.personal: I hope your garden is growing well.

options: Thank you so much for the book about birds.
thanks.why: Name the gift, so the giver knows you noticed it.

options: I read the part about owls twice, and now I want to see one!
I already had one, but that is okay.
detail.why: Say how you will use or enjoy it.

blocks.title: Writing the note
blocks.q: Omar got a soccer ball from his Aunt Rosa. Write a short thank-you note.
steps: Greeting: “Dear Aunt Rosa,”
Thanks for the specific gift: “Thank you for the soccer ball.”
How he will use it: “I already took it to practice, and Coach liked it too.” A personal line: “I hope I see you at my next game.”
Closing and signature: “Love, Omar”
blocks.a: “Dear Aunt Rosa, Thank you for the soccer ball. I already took it to practice. I hope I see you at my next game. Love, Omar”

blocks.title: Addressing the envelope
blocks.q: Hana mails her note to Dr. Bell. Where does each part go on the envelope?
steps: Dr. Bell’s name and address go in the center.
Hana’s own address, the return address, goes in the upper left corner.
The stamp goes in the upper right corner.
blocks.a: Delivery address in the center, return address upper left, stamp upper right.

blocks.cap: Where everything goes on an envelope.

blocks.html: Writing “Thanks for the gift” without naming it, or waiting months. Name the gift, add one real detail, and send it within a week or two.
