blocks.html: Everyone makes mistakes: a sharp word, a broken promise, a borrowed book returned with a torn cover. What matters is what you do next. A good apology can repair a friendship faster than almost anything else.

A good apology says what you did, says you are sorry without a “but,” offers to make it right, and is followed by doing better next time. “I’m sorry I yelled at you during the game. That wasn’t fair. I’ll keep my cool next time.”

An apology is for the person who was hurt. Naming what you did shows you understand it. A “but” (“Sorry, but you started it”) turns the apology into a defense and puts the blame back on them. Offering to fix things, and then changing, shows that the words were meant.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: The parts of a good apology
items: Say what you did: “I borrowed your book and the cover tore.”
Say you’re sorry, with no “but”: “I’m really sorry.”
Offer to make it right: “Can I buy you a new one, or tape it?”
Say what you’ll do next time: “I’ll be more careful with things I borrow.”

blocks.cap: Put the parts in order, then Check.

blocks.title: A sharp word
blocks.q: At lunch, Leo made fun of Sam’s drawing, and Sam looked hurt. What could Leo say?
steps: Name it: “I made fun of your drawing.”
Say sorry with no excuse: “I’m sorry. That was mean.”
Make it right and do better: “It’s actually really good. I won’t do that again.”
blocks.a: “I’m sorry I made fun of your drawing. That was mean, and I won’t do it again.”

blocks.title: Fixing an apology
blocks.q: Ruby forgot to save Mia a seat as she promised and said, “Sorry you feel that way.” How could she apologize better?
steps: “Sorry you feel that way” blames Mia’s feelings instead of owning the broken promise.
Name what she did: “I forgot to save you a seat after I promised.”
Say sorry and offer a fix: “I’m sorry. I’ll save you one tomorrow.”
blocks.a: “I’m sorry I forgot to save you a seat after I promised. I’ll save you one tomorrow.”

blocks.html: Saying “I’m sorry you feel that way” or “Sorry, but you started it.” Those blame the other person. Own your part. A quick check: does your apology have the word “I” and no “but”?
Accepting an apology is a courtesy too. “Thanks for saying that” or “It’s okay, I forgive you” lets you both move on. If you aren’t ready yet, “Thank you. I need a little time” is honest and kind.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: Friends won’t always agree, about a movie, a rule, a game plan or a bigger idea. Disagreeing is not rude. Like apologizing well, doing it kindly is a skill.

Disagree with the idea, not the person. Listen first, say what you agree with, then give your view with “I think” instead of “You’re wrong.” “I see why you like that plan. I think we’d have more time if we left earlier.”

People defend themselves when they feel attacked, and then nobody listens. Talking about the idea keeps the other person’s dignity safe. Starting with what you agree with shows you heard them, and “I think” makes it clear you are sharing a view, not handing down a ruling. You can disagree and still be friends.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: “I see your point. I think the blue poster is easier to read.”
“That’s a dumb idea.”
cards.why: It attacks the person, not the idea.

cards.text: “What makes you think that? I see it differently.”
“You’re wrong, as usual.”
cards.why: “As usual” turns a disagreement into a put-down.

cards.text: “We can agree to disagree.”
Rolling your eyes while a friend explains.
cards.why: Listen first, even when you disagree.

blocks.cap: Sort each response, then Check.

blocks.title: A group project
blocks.q: Omar wants their project poster to be about volcanoes. Hana thinks earthquakes would be better. What could Hana say?
steps: Listen and find something to agree with: “Volcanoes would look great.”
Give her view with “I think”: “I think earthquakes might be easier, because we already have the library book.”
Invite a solution: “Could we do both, or flip a coin?”
blocks.a: “Volcanoes would look great. I think earthquakes might be easier, since we have the book. Want to do both?”

blocks.title: Disagreeing with a grown-up
blocks.q: Grandpa Walt says the old movie is better than the new one. Sam disagrees. How can he say so respectfully?
steps: Ask about Grandpa’s view first: “What did you like about the old one?”
Share his own: “I think the new one’s effects are amazing.”
Keep it friendly; it is a conversation, not a contest.
blocks.a: “What did you like about the old one? I think the new one’s effects are amazing.”

blocks.html: Thinking disagreeing is rude, or that winning the argument is the goal. You can disagree and still be friends. The goal is understanding each other, and sometimes agreeing to disagree.

Some topics, like politics and religion, can stir strong feelings. With friends and family, it is fine to say, “Let’s talk about something else,” and that is often the kindest choice at a party or a meal.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: Games are more fun when everyone plays well together, whether it is a league game, a pickup game at recess or a board game at home. Sportsmanship is the set of manners that makes that happen.
Play fair, accept the referee’s calls, cheer for your team without jeering the other one, and shake hands after the game, win or lose: “Good game.”

A game only works if both sides agree to the rules and to the people who enforce them. Arguing every call or mocking the other team turns a game into a fight. A good sport is gracious in winning, because the other team worked hard too, and gracious in losing, because the winners earned it.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Saying “Good game” to every player in the handshake line.
Yelling at the referee after a call.
cards.why: Accept the call; your coach can ask about it.

cards.text: Helping up a player from the other team who fell.
Doing a dance in the other team’s faces after a goal.
cards.why: Celebrate with your team, not at the other one.

cards.text: Cheering for your team.
Quitting the board game when you start losing.
cards.why: Finish the game; the others are counting on you.

blocks.cap: Sort each action, then Check.

blocks.title: A bad call
blocks.q: In Mia’s softball game, the umpire calls her out at first base. She is sure she was safe. What should she do?
steps: Accept the call and jog back to the dugout.
Don’t argue or throw her helmet.
If it matters, her coach can ask the umpire calmly; that is the coach’s job.
blocks.a: Accept the call and let the coach handle any question.

blocks.title: Winning big
blocks.q: Leo’s team wins 8 to 1. What does gracious winning look like?
steps: Celebrate with his own team, not at the other team.
Shake hands and say “Good game” to every player.
Say something kind if he can: “You guys played hard.”
blocks.a: Celebrate with his team, then shake hands and say “Good game.”

blocks.html: Arguing every call, or celebrating by mocking the other team. A good sport is gracious in both winning and losing. Check: would you be glad to play against yourself?
Customs differ. Leagues use different end-of-game customs: a handshake line, high fives, a fist bump or a cheer for the other team. Follow your team’s custom; the idea is the same.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: School is a place where many people share a room for many hours. The skills from disagreeing kindly help a lot, and so do a few classroom habits that teachers notice every day.
Greet your teacher, raise your hand and wait to be called on, listen when others speak, and ask for help respectfully. If you disagree with a grade or a rule, ask to talk after class.

A teacher is trying to help twenty or thirty people learn at once. Raising your hand gives everyone a fair turn, and listening to classmates gives their ideas the same respect you want for yours. Talking about a grade in private keeps it calm and lets the teacher listen, without an audience.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.prompt: Ms. Park asks a question. Omar knows the answer right away. What should he do?

choices.text: Raise his hand and wait to be called on.
choices.outcome: Everyone gets a chance to think, and Omar gets his turn.

choices.text: Shout out the answer.
choices.outcome: Hana was still thinking. Calling out takes away everyone else’s turn.

choices.text: Whisper the answer to Hana.
choices.outcome: Whispering distracts both of them. Raise your hand instead.

blocks.cap: Choose what Omar does.

blocks.title: A grade that seems wrong
blocks.q: Sam thinks a test question was marked wrong by mistake. What is the respectful way to handle it?
steps: Wait until after class, or ask, “Could I talk with you about my test sometime?”
Bring the test and explain calmly: “I think this answer might be right. Could you look again?”
Accept the teacher’s answer politely, even if it is not the one he hoped for.
blocks.a: Ask to talk privately after class, and explain calmly.

blocks.title: Asking for help
blocks.q: Ruby doesn’t understand the homework. What can she say?
steps: Ask at a good moment, such as after class or during work time.
Be specific: “Ms. Park, I’m stuck on number 4. Could you explain the first step?”
Thank her for the help.
blocks.a: “Ms. Park, I’m stuck on number 4. Could you explain the first step? Thank you!”

blocks.html: Calling out answers, or arguing about a grade in front of the class. Raise your hand and wait; for grades, ask to talk after class.
Small courtesies count: say good morning and goodbye, hold the door, help a substitute learn names, and return borrowed supplies.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: You have learned to show respect at school. Older people, like grandparents, neighbors and family friends, deserve that respect too, and showing it is one of the warmest things you can do.
Offer older people your seat, your help with doors and bags, and your attention. Listen to their stories, ask them questions, and stand when they enter.

Older people have spent a lifetime working, raising families and learning things you haven’t yet. Small courtesies like a seat or a held door make their day easier. And your attention is a gift: many older people love to share their stories, and they don’t always find someone who wants to hear them.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Offering your seat on a crowded bus to an older man.
Rolling your eyes at Grandpa’s old stories.
cards.why: Ask a question instead. His stories are part of your family’s history.

cards.text: Asking Grandma what school was like when she was young.
Carrying a neighbor’s grocery bag to her door.
Calling an older neighbor by a nickname without asking.
cards.why: Use the name and title they prefer.

cards.text: Looking at your phone while Grandpa talks.
cards.why: Put it down and give him your attention.

blocks.cap: Sort each action, then Check.

blocks.title: Asking about a life
blocks.q: Hana is visiting her great-aunt, who doesn’t say much. What could Hana ask?
steps: Open questions about her life work best: “What was your first job?”
Or about the past: “What did you do for fun when you were my age?”
Then listen, and ask a follow-up about what she says.
blocks.a: “What did you do for fun when you were my age?” Then listen and ask more.

blocks.html: Thinking respect means staying silent around older people. Asking an older relative about their life is one of the kindest things you can do. Respect is attention, help and interest, not silence.

Customs differ. Families and cultures show respect to elders in many ways: special titles, bowing, serving elders first at meals, kissing a hand, or using formal words. Learn your family’s ways, and when you visit others, follow theirs.

blocks.html: Family manners are the ones we practice most, with the people we see every day. It is easy to be polite to guests and forget the people at home, but home is where manners matter most.
Do your share of the chores without being asked twice, notice what needs doing and do it, and thank family members for what they do for you.

A home runs on many small jobs: dishes, laundry, trash, feeding the dog. When everyone helps, nobody carries all of it. Noticing a job and doing it without being asked is a way of saying, “I’m part of this family too.” And thanks at home matter just as much as thanks anywhere else.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: Clearing the table after dinner
items: Ask to be excused, or wait until everyone has finished.
Carry your own plate and silverware to the kitchen.
Scrape leftovers into the trash or compost.
Bring in the serving dishes and wipe the table.
Thank the cook again on your way out.

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order, then Check.

blocks.title: Noticing a job
blocks.q: Leo walks past the full trash can on his way to his room. Taking out the trash is his sister’s chore this week. What could he do?
steps: Notice it: the bag is full and she is at practice.
Take it out, or at least tell someone it’s full.
No need to make a big deal; small help is the point.
blocks.a: Take it out anyway, or let someone know.

blocks.html: Helping only when it is “your” chore. Family manners are the ones we practice most. Check: when you see something that needs doing, do you do it?
Thank-yous at home: “Thanks for driving me, Mom.” “Thanks for helping me with my homework, Grandpa.” They are short, and they make a home feel kinder.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: Lines are everywhere: at the cafeteria, the ticket booth, the bus stop, the bathroom at halftime. A line is a simple, fair system, and it only works when everyone in it plays fair.
Join a line at the end, leave a little space in front of you, keep your bag close, and don’t save places for friends who arrive later.

A line is first come, first served, which is fair to everyone. Each person who joins in front of you makes everyone behind you wait longer, even if it is “just one friend.” A little space and a bag held close keep you from bumping people in a crowd, where everyone is already short on room.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Walking to the end of the line.
Waving three friends into your spot near the front.
cards.why: Everyone behind you now waits longer.

cards.text: Holding your backpack in front of you in a crowd.
Standing so close you bump the person ahead.
cards.why: Leave a little space.

cards.text: Moving up when the line moves.
Pretending not to see the line and walking to the front.
cards.why: Cutting is unfair to everyone who waited.

blocks.cap: Sort each action as polite or rude, then Check.

blocks.title: Friends arrive late
blocks.q: Sam is near the front of the line for the school play tickets. His friends Leo and Omar arrive and want to join him. What should Sam do?
steps: Saving places for friends who just arrived isn’t fair to the people behind him.
Kindly say, “The line starts back there. I’ll wait for you inside.”
Or Sam can go to the back with them, if he wants to stay together.
blocks.a: “The line starts back there. I’ll wait for you inside.”

blocks.title: A crowded hallway
blocks.q: After an assembly, the hallway is packed. How can Ruby move through it politely?
steps: Keep to the right and move with the crowd.
Hold her bag in front of her.
If she bumps someone, say “Excuse me” or “Sorry.”
blocks.a: Keep right, bag close, and “excuse me” if she bumps someone.

blocks.html: Thinking saving spots for friends is fine. Each person who joins in front of you makes everyone behind you wait longer. If you want to be with your friends, join them at the back.

Customs differ. Holding one place for someone who steps away for a moment (to grab a napkin or use the restroom) and asks you to is widely accepted. Letting a group of late friends in is not. In some countries, lines work a little differently; follow what people around you do.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: Doors and elevators are where people meet in small spaces. Like lines, they work best with a few simple customs that keep people from bumping into one another.
Hold a door for the person right behind you. Let people off an elevator before you get on. Offer to press the button for others, and stand aside to make room.

Holding a door takes two seconds and saves the next person from a door swinging into them, especially if their hands are full. People inside an elevator need to get out before there is room for anyone to get in, so waiting to the side actually makes things faster for everyone.

blocks.name: et-order

opts.title: Taking the elevator
items: Stand to the side of the doors while you wait.
Let everyone get off first.
Step in and move toward the back.
Ask, “Which floor?” and press the button for others.
Step aside at each stop so people can get out.

blocks.cap: Put the steps in order, then Check.

blocks.title: Hands full
blocks.q: Hana sees Mr. Diaz coming toward the library door with a big box. What should she do?
steps: Hold the door open for him and stand to the side.
Wait until he is through.
He will likely say “Thank you”; she can answer, “You’re welcome.”
blocks.a: Hold the door open and stand aside until he’s through.

blocks.title: The elevator opens
blocks.q: At the doctor’s office, the elevator doors open and three people are inside, about to get off. Leo is in a hurry. What should he do?
steps: Step to the side of the doors.
Let all three people get off.
Then step in, move to the back, and press his floor.
blocks.a: Step aside, let them off, then get on.

blocks.html: Rushing into an elevator as soon as the doors open. The people inside can’t get out, and everyone is slowed down. Step aside and let people out first.
If someone holds a door for you, say thank you. If the person behind you is far away, you don’t need to wait; a door held too long can make them rush.
Customs differ. On escalators in many American cities, people stand on the right and walk on the left. Not every place does this, so watch what people around you do.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: Sidewalks, hallways, trails and park paths are shared by everyone: walkers, strollers, people in wheelchairs, dog walkers, runners. The same fairness as lines and crowds keeps everyone moving.
Walk on the right. In a group, don’t spread out across the whole path. If you need to stop or check your phone, step to the side. And clean up after yourself.

When everyone keeps right, people going opposite ways pass easily. A group walking four across forces others into the street or the grass. Stopping in the middle of a busy path is like stopping in a doorway: everyone behind you has to swerve. Litter left behind becomes someone else’s job.

blocks.name: et-sort

cards.text: Walking on the right side of the path.
Walking four across so no one can pass.
cards.why: Pair up or go single file when others need to pass.

cards.text: Stepping to the side to text.
Stopping in a doorway to chat.
cards.why: Step out of the way first.

cards.text: Throwing your wrapper in a trash can.
Leaving your scooter in the middle of the sidewalk.
cards.why: Someone could trip over it.

blocks.cap: Sort each habit, then Check.

blocks.title: A group walk
blocks.q: Mia, Sam and Ruby are walking side by side on a sidewalk when a woman with a stroller comes toward them. What should they do?
steps: Move into single file or two by two on the right.
Leave room for the stroller to pass.
Then spread back out once she has passed, if there is room.
blocks.a: Single file on the right until the stroller passes.

blocks.title: Checking directions
blocks.q: Omar needs to look at a map on his phone while walking in a busy downtown area. What should he do?
steps: Step to the side, out of the flow of people, next to a wall or a bench.
Check the map.
Then step back into the flow and keep right.
blocks.a: Step to the side to check, then rejoin the flow.

blocks.html: Stopping in the middle of a busy walkway or doorway. If you need to stop, step to the side, so the people behind you can keep going.
On a shared path, people on bikes often say “On your left” before they pass. If you hear it, keep to the right. Pick up after a dog you are walking, too.

sources.name: Present-day American etiquette as commonly taught to children and families (summarized in our own words)

blocks.html: A movie, a play, a concert or a recital is something many people share at once in the dark. It is a shared space too, and the people around you paid for the same experience you did.
Arrive on time, silence your phone and keep the screen dark, save talking for afterward, and clap at the right moments.

In a dark theater, even a small light or a whisper pulls people’s attention away from the show. A phone screen shines right into the eyes of the people behind you. Arriving on time means you don’t climb past people after the show starts. And applause is how an audience thanks the performers.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.prompt: The movie has started, and Leo’s phone buzzes. What should he do?

choices.text: Leave it in his pocket and check it after the movie.
choices.outcome: The theater stays dark, and nobody misses a moment.

choices.text: Check it quickly with the screen turned down low.
choices.outcome: Even a dim screen is bright in a dark theater, and the people behind see it.

choices.text: Whisper to Ruby about the message.
choices.outcome: Whispers carry. Save it for after the show.

blocks.cap: Choose what Leo does.

blocks.title: Arriving late to a play
blocks.q: Hana arrives at the school play just after it has started. What should she do?
steps: Wait at the back or the door until there is a break, or until an usher shows her to a seat.
Move quietly along the row and say “Excuse me” softly to the people she passes.
Sit quickly and keep her phone off.
blocks.a: Wait for a break or an usher, then slip quietly to a seat.

blocks.title: When to clap
blocks.q: At a band concert, Omar isn’t sure when to clap. What can he do?
steps: At a concert, people usually clap when a whole piece is finished.
At a play, people clap at the end of a scene, a song or the show.
When in doubt, wait and clap when others do.
blocks.a: Clap when the piece or scene ends, and follow the audience when unsure.

blocks.html: Whispering through a movie or checking your phone, whose light bothers the people behind you. Phone off and away, talking afterward.
A few more theater courtesies: unwrap snacks before the show starts, keep your feet off the seat in front, and if you must leave in the middle, go quietly at a pause.

blocks.html: At assemblies, ball games and ceremonies, you will often hear the Pledge of Allegiance or “The Star-Spangled Banner,” the national anthem. The United States Code, the collection of federal laws, describes the customs for both.

During the Pledge and the anthem, people stand, face the flag and place the right hand over the heart. The Code asks men not in uniform to remove hats other than religious head coverings, and today most people remove hats. People in uniform salute. If no flag is displayed during the anthem, face the music.

Standing still and quiet together is a shared sign of respect for the country and the people who serve it. It is also a courtesy to everyone around you: during those moments, talking or wandering distracts the people who are taking part.

What the U.S. Code describes

Stand facing the flag, right hand over the heart; men not in uniform remove headdress other than religious head coverings; people in uniform face the flag and salute.
The national anthem (36 U.S.C. § 301)
With the flag displayed: face the flag, stand at attention, right hand over the heart. With no flag: face toward the music.
The flag passing in a parade, or being raised or lowered (4 U.S.C. § 9)
Face the flag, stand at attention, right hand over the heart.
blocks.cap: What the Code describes for civilians.

blocks.name: et-scene

opts.narr: Before the game, everyone stands for the anthem.

blocks.cap: Right hand over the heart, facing the flag.

blocks.title: At a ball game
blocks.q: Sam is wearing a baseball cap at a game when the anthem begins. What does the custom ask?
steps: Stand and face the flag.
Take off the cap; today most people do, and the Code asks it of men not in uniform.
Hold the cap with the right hand over the heart, or put the hand over the heart, and stay quiet until the song ends.
blocks.a: Stand, face the flag, cap off, right hand over the heart.

blocks.title: No flag in sight
blocks.q: At an indoor event, the anthem plays but there is no flag in the room. What should Mia do?
steps: Stand.
Face toward the music, as 36 U.S.C. § 301 describes.
Right hand over the heart until the song ends.
blocks.a: Stand, face the music, right hand over the heart.

blocks.html: Keeping a hat on or talking during the anthem. When no flag is displayed, people face the music. The Code describes customs; it does not punish anyone for not following them.

Some people choose not to say the Pledge, for reasons of belief. In 1943 the Supreme Court decided that public schools cannot require students to say it. Respecting other people’s choices quietly is part of good manners too.

blocks.html: After the Pledge and the anthem, the Flag Code’s best-known rules are about how the flag is displayed. One idea explains most of them: the flag’s place of honor is at the top and to the flag’s own right.
On a wall, horizontal or vertical, the flag’s blue union (the field of stars) goes at the top and to the flag’s own right, which is the viewer’s left. On a staff, the union is at the peak.

In many traditions, the right side is the place of honor, as when a guest of honor sits at the host’s right. The union is the flag’s honored part, so it goes uppermost and at the flag’s own right. Imagine the flag as a person facing you: its right hand is on your left.

blocks.name: et-flag
blocks.cap: Tap the picture that follows the Flag Code, then Check.

head: Where the flag is
The rule (4 U.S.C. § 7)
rows: On a wall, horizontal or vertical
Union at the top, at the flag’s own right: the viewer’s left (§ 7(i)).
In a window
The same way, union to the left of a person looking from the street (§ 7(i)).
On a speaker’s platform, on a staff
At the speaker’s right as they face the audience (§ 7(k)).
Crossed staffs with another flag
The U.S. flag on its own right, its staff in front (§ 7(d)).
blocks.cap: A few display rules.

blocks.title: Hanging it vertically
blocks.q: Ruby’s class wants to hang the flag vertically on the wall behind the teacher’s desk. Where does the union go?
steps: Vertical or horizontal, the rule is the same: the union is at the top.
It is at the flag’s own right, which is the viewer’s left.
So as the class looks at it, the stars are at the top left.
blocks.a: At the top, on the left as the class looks at it.

blocks.title: A flag on a pole
blocks.q: At a scout meeting, Omar raises the flag on a pole. Where does the union go?
steps: On a staff, the union goes at the peak, the top, next to the pole.
The Code adds that the flag is raised briskly and lowered slowly and ceremoniously (§ 6(b)).
The flag is never flown upside down except as a signal of dire distress (§ 8(a)).
blocks.a: At the top of the pole, next to the staff.

blocks.name: et-flag
blocks.cap: On a platform, the flag stands at the speaker’s right.

blocks.html: Hanging a vertical flag with the union at the top right, as seen from the front. Whichever way it hangs on a wall, the union is at the top left as you look at it.

blocks.html: Besides how to display the flag, the Flag Code describes how to care for it. These customs treat the flag the way you would treat something that matters to many people.

The Flag Code asks that the flag not touch anything beneath it, such as the ground or the floor; that it fly from sunrise to sunset unless it is lit at night; and that a flag too worn to fly be retired in a dignified way, preferably by burning.

Each custom is a sign of care: keeping the flag off the ground keeps it clean and shows respect; lighting it at night keeps it visible when it flies; and retiring a worn flag with dignity, instead of throwing it in the trash, honors what it stands for. Many groups, such as veterans’ organizations and scout troops, hold flag retirement ceremonies.

blocks.name: et-flag
blocks.cap: Use Next to see how a flag is put at half-staff.

items: Keep it from touching the ground or floor (4 U.S.C. § 8(b)).
Fly it from sunrise to sunset, or day and night if it is lit after dark (§ 6(a)).
Don’t fly it in bad weather unless it is an all-weather flag (§ 6(c)).
For half-staff, raise it to the peak for an instant, then lower it to half-staff; raise it to the peak again before lowering it for the day (§ 7(m)).
Retire a worn flag in a dignified way, preferably by burning (§ 8(k)).

blocks.title: A flag touches the ground
blocks.q: While folding the class flag, Leo and Hana let a corner touch the floor. Does the flag have to be destroyed?
steps: No. The Code asks that the flag be kept from touching the ground; it does not say a flag that touches it must be destroyed.
Pick it up, check that it is clean and undamaged.
A clean, undamaged flag can still be flown.
blocks.a: No. Pick it up; if it is clean and undamaged, it can still be flown.

blocks.title: Night-time
blocks.q: Sam’s family wants to leave their flag up overnight. What does the Code say?
steps: The custom is to fly the flag from sunrise to sunset.
It may fly day and night if it is properly lit after dark.
So they can leave it up if a light shines on it.
blocks.a: Leave it up only if it is lit at night.

blocks.html: Thinking a flag that touches the ground must be destroyed. The Code asks only that it be kept from touching the ground; a clean, undamaged flag can still be flown. The Code is guidance for civilians and has no penalties.
